# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

## PART A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1 [KTU University Exam – May 2024]
**Differentiate between Forward Kinematics and Inverse Kinematics in robotics.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| Aspect | Forward Kinematics | Inverse Kinematics |
|---|---|---|
| **Input** | Joint angles $\theta_i$ | End-effector pose $(x, y, z, \phi, \theta, \psi)$ |
| **Output** | End-effector pose | Required joint angles $\theta_i$ |
| **Solution** | Always unique; closed-form | Multiple solutions possible |
| **Computational** | Simple matrix multiplication | Non-linear, iterative or closed-form |
| **Difficulty** | Easy, direct | Hard, requires geometric insight |
| **Equation** | $T = \prod A_i(\theta_i)$ | $\theta = IK(T_{desired})$ |

*(1 mark each for clear definition, input/output mapping, and uniqueness/multiplicity comparison.)*

---

### Question 2 [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]
**List and briefly explain any three characteristics of an ideal sensor used in robotic applications.**

**Model Answer (3 marks — 1 mark per characteristic):**

1. **Accuracy:** The sensor output must closely match the true physical value being measured. High-accuracy sensors minimize systematic error. *(1 mark)*

2. **Sensitivity:** Defined as the ratio of change in output to change in input ($S = \Delta y / \Delta x$). An ideal sensor has high sensitivity to detect small input variations. *(1 mark)*

3. **Linearity:** The output should be linearly proportional to the input over the full range. Linearity simplifies calibration and controller design. *(1 mark)*

*(Alternative accepted characteristics: resolution, repeatability, bandwidth, linearity, hysteresis.)*

---

## PART B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each)

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall Callout:**
> - In DH problems, students often forget to **assign the base frame correctly** (Z₀ along joint 1 axis, X₀ perpendicular to Z₀ and Z₁). This single mistake cascades and loses 4–5 marks.
> - In dynamics, do NOT forget the **gravity term** $G(\theta)$ — it is the most commonly omitted term.
> - In PID tuning, always **state the stability condition** explicitly (Routh–Hurwitz check) — the examiner allocates 2 marks specifically for this.
> - Use **units in every step**. A numerical answer without units loses one mark.
> - Avoid using the vertical pipe `|` symbol for absolute value inside LaTeX — use `\vert` or `\mid` instead.

---

### Question A (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam – May 2024]

**(a)** For a 2-link planar manipulator with link lengths $l_1$ and $l_2$, derive the **Forward Kinematics** using the DH convention. Clearly state the DH parameter table and write the final homogeneous transformation matrix $T_2^0$. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** For the same manipulator, derive the **Jacobian matrix** $J(\theta)$ using the direct differentiation method, and identify the **singular configurations** of the manipulator. **(7 marks)**

---

#### Model Solution for Question A(a)

**Step 1 — DH Parameter Table (2 marks):**

| Link $i$ | $a_i$ | $\alpha_i$ | $d_i$ | $\theta_i$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $l_1$ | $0$ | $0$ | $\theta_1$ |
| 2 | $l_2$ | $0$ | $0$ | $\theta_2$ |

**Step 2 — Compute $A_1$ and $A_2$ matrices (3 marks):**

Using the standard DH formula with $\alpha = 0$:

$$A_1 = \begin{bmatrix} c_1 & -s_1 & 0 & l_1 c_1 \\ s_1 & c_1 & 0 & l_1 s_1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad A_2 = \begin{bmatrix} c_2 & -s_2 & 0 & l_2 c_2 \\ s_2 & c_2 & 0 & l_2 s_2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 3 — Multiply $A_1 A_2$ (2 marks):**

$$T_2^0 = \begin{bmatrix} c_{12} & -s_{12} & 0 & l_1 c_1 + l_2 c_{12} \\ s_{12} & c_{12} & 0 & l_1 s_1 + l_2 s_{12} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

where $c_{12} = \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$ and $s_{12} = \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$. Hence the end-effector position is $(x, y) = (l_1 c_1 + l_2 c_{12},\ l_1 s_1 + l_2 s_{12})$ and orientation is $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ about the z-axis. ✓

---

#### Model Solution for Question A(b)

**Step 1 — Position equations (2 marks):**

$$x = l_1 \cos\theta_1 + l_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$$
$$y = l_1 \sin\theta_1 + l_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$$

**Step 2 — Differentiate (3 marks):**

$$\dot{x} = -l_1 s_1 \dot\theta_1 - l_2 s_{12}(\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)$$
$$\dot{y} = l_1 c_1 \dot\theta_1 + l_2 c_{12}(\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)$$

Rearranging in matrix form:
$$\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -l_1 s_1 - l_2 s_{12} & -l_2 s_{12} \\ l_1 c_1 + l_2 c_{12} & l_2 c_{12} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dot\theta_1 \\ \dot\theta_2 \end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 3 — Jacobian and singularity (2 marks):**

$$J(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} -l_1 s_1 - l_2 s_{12} & -l_2 s_{12} \\ l_1 c_1 + l_2 c_{12} & l_2 c_{12} \end{bmatrix}$$

The determinant is:
$$\det(J) = (-l_1 s_1 - l_2 s_{12})(l_2 c_{12}) - (-l_2 s_{12})(l_1 c_1 + l_2 c_{12})$$

Expanding:
$$= -l_1 l_2 s_1 c_{12} - l_2^2 s_{12} c_{12} + l_1 l_2 s_{12} c_1 + l_2^2 s_{12} c_{12}$$
$$= l_1 l_2 (s_{12} c_1 - s_1 c_{12}) = l_1 l_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2 - \theta_1) = l_1 l_2 \sin\theta_2$$

**Singularities occur when** $\det(J) = 0$, i.e., when $\sin\theta_2 = 0$:

- $\theta_2 = 0$: arm is **fully stretched outward** — boundary of workspace.
- $\theta_2 = \pi$: arm is **fully folded back** — degenerate configuration.

At these configurations, the manipulator loses one DOF in Cartesian space and joint velocities become theoretically infinite for finite end-effector velocities. ✓

---

### Question B (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]

**(a)** Explain the **Lagrangian formulation** of robot dynamics. Derive the **generalized torque equation** $\tau = M(\theta)\ddot{\theta} + C(\theta, \dot{\theta})\dot{\theta} + G(\theta) + \tau_{friction}$ from first principles. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** A DC servo motor has armature resistance $R = 2\ \Omega$, torque constant $K_t = 0.05\ \text{Nm/A}$, back-EMF constant $K_b = 0.05\ \text{V·s/rad}$, and armature inductance $L = 5\ \text{mH}$. The motor drives a load of inertia $J = 1 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{kg·m}^2$ and viscous friction coefficient $b = 1 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{Nm·s/rad}$. A PID controller is used with gains $K_p = 10$, $K_i = 5$, $K_d = 0.1$. Determine the **closed-loop transfer function** $\Theta(s)/V(s)$ and check its **stability** using the Routh–Hurwitz criterion. **(7 marks)**

---

#### Model Solution for Question B(a)

**Step 1 — Define the Lagrangian (2 marks):**

The Lagrangian of a robotic system is the difference between total kinetic energy $K$ and total potential energy $V$:

$$L(\theta, \dot\theta) = K(\theta, \dot\theta) - V(\theta)$$

For a single link rotating about a fixed axis with moment of inertia $I(\theta)$ (which may depend on configuration in multi-link systems), the kinetic energy is:

$$K = \frac{1}{2} \dot\theta^T M(\theta) \dot\theta$$

The potential energy is $V(\theta)$, typically due to gravity acting on link centers of mass.

**Step 2 — Euler–Lagrange equation (2 marks):**

For each generalized coordinate $\theta_i$, the equation of motion is:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot\theta_i}\right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_i} = Q_i$$

where $Q_i$ is the generalized non-conservative force (the actuator torque $\tau_i$, minus friction).

**Step 3 — Derive the matrix form (3 marks):**

Substituting the kinetic energy expression:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot\theta_i} = \sum_j M_{ij}(\theta) \dot\theta_j$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot\theta_i}\right) = \sum_j M_{ij} \ddot\theta_j + \sum_j \sum_k \frac{\partial M_{ij}}{\partial \theta_k} \dot\theta_k \dot\theta_j$$

Also, $\frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_i} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j,k} \frac{\partial M_{jk}}{\partial \theta_i} \dot\theta_j \dot\theta_k - \frac{\partial V}{\partial \theta_i}$.

Combining and using the Christoffel symbol identity:
$$\sum_j \sum_k \left(\frac{\partial M_{ij}}{\partial \theta_k} - \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial M_{jk}}{\partial \theta_i}\right) \dot\theta_j \dot\theta_k = \sum_j C_{ij}(\theta, \dot\theta) \dot\theta_j$$

The final compact form is:

$$\boxed{\tau = M(\theta)\ddot\theta + C(\theta, \dot\theta)\dot\theta + G(\theta) + \tau_{friction}}$$

where:
- $M(\theta)$ = mass/inertia matrix, symmetric and positive definite,
- $C(\theta, \dot\theta)$ = Coriolis and centripetal matrix,
- $G(\theta) = \partial V/\partial \theta$ = gravity vector,
- $\tau_{friction}$ = friction torque. ✓

---

#### Model Solution for Question B(b)

**Step 1 — Motor Transfer Function (3 marks):**

The DC motor equations in the Laplace domain:
$$V(s) = (R + Ls)I(s) + K_b s \Theta(s)$$
$$\tau_m(s) = K_t I(s) = (J s^2 + b s)\Theta(s)$$

From the second equation: $I(s) = (J s^2 + b s)\Theta(s)/K_t$.

Substituting into the first:
$$V(s) = (R + Ls)\frac{(J s^2 + b s)\Theta(s)}{K_t} + K_b s \Theta(s)$$

Dividing by $\Theta(s)$ and rearranging:
$$G_m(s) = \frac{\Theta(s)}{V(s)} = \frac{K_t}{s[L J s^2 + (L b + R J) s + (R b + K_t K_b)]}$$

Plugging in numerical values:
- $LJ = (5 \times 10^{-3})(10^{-4}) = 5 \times 10^{-7}$
- $Lb + RJ = (5 \times 10^{-3})(10^{-5}) + 2 \cdot 10^{-4} = 5 \times 10^{-8} + 2 \times 10^{-4} = 2.00005 \times 10^{-4}$
- $Rb + K_t K_b = 2 \cdot 10^{-5} + 0.0025 = 0.00252$
- $K_t = 0.05$

$$G_m(s) = \frac{0.05}{s(5 \times 10^{-7} s^2 + 2 \times 10^{-4} s + 0.00252)}$$

**Step 2 — Closed-Loop Transfer Function with PID (2 marks):**

The PID controller is $C(s) = \frac{K_d s^2 + K_p s + K_i}{s} = \frac{0.1 s^2 + 10 s + 5}{s}$.

The closed-loop transfer function is $T(s) = \frac{C(s) G_m(s)}{1 + C(s) G_m(s)}$.

Computing the denominator $1 + C(s) G_m(s)$:
$$1 + \frac{0.05(0.1 s^2 + 10 s + 5)}{s^2(5 \times 10^{-7} s^2 + 2 \times 10^{-4} s + 0.00252)}$$

After expansion and simplification (characteristic polynomial of degree 4):
$$5 \times 10^{-7} s^4 + 2 \times 10^{-4} s^3 + (0.00252 + 0.005) s^2 + 0.5 s + 0.25$$
$$= 5 \times 10^{-7} s^4 + 2 \times 10^{-4} s^3 + 0.00752 s^2 + 0.5 s + 0.25$$

**Step 3 — Routh–Hurwitz Stability Check (2 marks):**

For the polynomial $a_4 s^4 + a_3 s^3 + a_2 s^2 + a_1 s + a_0$:
- $a_4 = 5 \times 10^{-7}$ ✓ positive
- $a_3 = 2 \times 10^{-4}$ ✓ positive
- $a_2 = 7.52 \times 10^{-3}$ ✓ positive
- $a_1 = 0.5$ ✓ positive
- $a_0 = 0.25$ ✓ positive

Constructing the Routh array:

| Row | Col 1 | Col 2 | Col 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| $s^4$ | $5 \times 10^{-7}$ | $7.52 \times 10^{-3}$ | $0.25$ |
| $s^3$ | $2 \times 10^{-4}$ | $0.5$ | $0$ |
| $s^2$ | $b_1$ | $b_2$ | |
| $s^1$ | $c_1$ | | |
| $s^0$ | $0.25$ | | |

where:
$$b_1 = \frac{(2 \times 10^{-4})(7.52 \times 10^{-3}) - (5 \times 10^{-7})(0.5)}{2 \times 10^{-4}} = \frac{1.504 \times 10^{-6} - 2.5 \times 10^{-7}}{2 \times 10^{-4}} = 6.27 \times 10^{-3}$$

$$b_2 = \frac{(2 \times 10^{-4})(0.25) - 0}{2 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.25$$

$$c_1 = \frac{(6.27 \times 10^{-3})(0.5) - (2 \times 10^{-4})(0.25)}{6.27 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{3.135 \times 10^{-3} - 5 \times 10^{-5}}{6.27 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 0.492$$

All first-column entries are positive ($5 \times 10^{-7},\ 2 \times 10^{-4},\ 6.27 \times 10^{-3},\ 0.492,\ 0.25$), so the system is **stable** by the Routh–Hurwitz criterion. ✓

---

## Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist for KTU 2024 ESE – Module 2**

- ✅ **Kinematics** is the geometry of motion; **Dynamics** is the physics of motion.
- ✅ **DH convention** uses **4 parameters per joint**: $\theta_i, d_i, a_i, \alpha_i$. The order of multiplication matters — always follow $R_z \to T_z \to T_x \to R_x$.
- ✅ The **Jacobian** maps joint velocity → Cartesian velocity ($\dot x = J \dot\theta$) and Cartesian force → joint torque ($\tau = J^T F$).
- ✅ **Singularities** occur where $\det(J) = 0$ — robot loses DOF; the manipulator cannot move in certain Cartesian directions.
- ✅ **Inverse Kinematics (IK)** can have multiple solutions (elbow-up vs elbow-down); FK has exactly one.
- ✅ The general robot dynamics equation is $\tau = M\ddot\theta + C\dot\theta + G + \tau_{f}$. The **Lagrangian method** uses $L = K - V$ and the Euler–Lagrange equation.
- ✅ **PID** has three actions: Proportional (present error), Integral (past error), Derivative (future/anticipated error). Closed-loop TF for unity feedback: $T = CG/(1+CG)$.
- ✅ **Routh–Hurwitz** is the KTU-preferred stability test for polynomial characteristic equations.
- ✅ **Sensors** are classified as *proprioceptive* (encoders, IMUs) and *exteroceptive* (cameras, LiDAR, force sensors).
- ✅ **Actuators** are classified by energy domain: *electric* (DC, stepper, BLDC), *hydraulic* (high force), *pneumatic* (fast, low force).
- ✅ For DC motors, **SI rule**: $K_t$ (Nm/A) = $K_b$ (V·s/rad) numerically.
- ✅ **Bandwidth**, **resolution**, and **repeatability** are the three most-quoted KTU sensor metrics.
- ✅ **Memorize the DH transformation matrix** — it is the single most-tested equation in this module.
- ✅ In every numerical answer, **include units** in the final boxed result.
- ✅ Use `\vert` or `\mid` (never `|`) for absolute value in LaTeX to avoid markdown table breaks.

## SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Robot Classification** is the systematic categorization of robotic manipulators and mobile systems based on three primary taxonomical parameters: **(1) Mechanical Geometry (Kinematic Configuration)**, **(2) Degrees of Freedom (DOF)**, and **(3) Application Domain (Functional Deployment)**. The classification is fundamental in KTU 2024 Scheme Robotics & Automation for selecting the appropriate manipulator architecture for a given industrial or research task, as each class exhibits distinct **workspace topology**, **payload capacity**, **stiffness profile**, and **path accuracy characteristics**.

The formal KTU 2024 syllabus (Module 2) defines robotic classification under the following three principal branches:

1. **Geometry-Based Classification** — Classification by the arrangement and type of joints (prismatic **P** vs. revolute **R**) forming the kinematic chain. The four classical architectures are **Cartesian (PPP)**, **Cylindrical (RPP)**, **Spherical/Polar (RRP)**, **Articulated (RRR)**, with extended modern categories including **SCARA (RRP — Selective Compliance)** and **Parallel/Delta** manipulators.

2. **Degrees of Freedom (DOF) Classification** — Classification by the number of independent positional and orientational parameters required to fully specify the end-effector pose in **3D Cartesian space (x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw)**. This is governed mathematically by the **Kutzbach–Grübler Criterion** for spatial mechanisms.

3. **Application-Based Classification** — Classification by the operational environment and intended functional use, spanning **Industrial Robotics, Medical Robotics, Military & Defense, Space Exploration, Underwater (ROV/AUV), Agricultural, Domestic, and Humanoid Robotics**.

---

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuitive Overview

> [!NOTE]
> **Plain English Explanation for First-Time Learners**

Imagine a robotic arm is like a **human arm**:

- The **shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints** are analogous to **revolute joints** (rotational, like bending your elbow).
- The **telescopic extension/retraction** of the arm is analogous to a **prismatic joint** (linear sliding, like a drawer).
- The **wrist** can rotate in multiple ways to orient the hand — this corresponds to additional **degrees of freedom**.

Just as humans have different body types suited for different sports (a swimmer's long arms vs. a wrestler's compact build), **robots come in different "body types" (geometries)** suited for different jobs. A **Cartesian robot** is like a **gantry crane** that moves only in straight lines — perfect for picking and placing boxes. An **articulated robot** is like a **human arm** — flexible enough to weld complex car body curves. A **SCARA robot** is like an arm that is very stiff vertically but compliant horizontally — perfect for rapid assembly of circuit boards.

> [!TIP]
> **Syllabus Highlight:** KTU frequently asks students to *match robot geometry to application* (e.g., "Which robot is best for palletizing?" or "Why is SCARA preferred for PCB assembly?"). Memorize the joint notation **PPP, RPP, RRP, RRR** — this is the *single most tested fact* in Module 2.

### 1.3 Key Terminology Master Table

| Term | Definition | Standard Notation |
|------|------------|-------------------|
| **Degrees of Freedom (DOF)** | Minimum number of independent parameters required to define the configuration of a mechanism in 3D space | $f$ or $n_{DOF}$ |
| **Prismatic Joint (P)** | A sliding joint that produces linear translation along a single axis | $\mathbf{P}$ |
| **Revolute Joint (R)** | A rotational/hinge joint that produces angular rotation about a single axis | $\mathbf{R}$ |
| **Workspace** | The total volume in 3D space reachable by the end-effector | $V_{ws}$ |
| **End-Effector** | The tool or gripper mounted at the tip of the manipulator | $E$ |
| **Payload** | Maximum mass the robot can carry at rated performance | $m_p$ (kg) |
| **Reach** | Maximum distance from the robot base to the end-effector center | $R$ (m) |
| **Repeatability** | The positional variation when returning to a pre-taught pose | $\pm \Delta r$ (mm) |

## SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Classification Based on Geometry (Kinematic Configuration)

The geometry of a robot is defined by the **sequence of joint types** in its kinematic chain, typically counted from the base (joint 1) to the end-effector. For a 3-primary-axis manipulator, the joint sequence fully describes its architecture.

#### 2.1.1 Cartesian Robot (PPP — Three Prismatic Joints)

- **Joint Notation:** **P-P-P** (all three primary joints are prismatic)
- **Axis Alignment:** Three mutually perpendicular linear axes (X, Y, Z)
- **Workspace Shape:** A rectangular cuboid box
- **Real-World Examples:** CNC gantry routers, 3D printers, pick-and-place machines
- **Advantages:** High positional accuracy, simple kinematics, easy to visualize
- **Disadvantages:** Requires large floor space, low flexibility, no orientation control without auxiliary wrist

> [!NOTE]
> **Kinematic Insight:** The forward kinematics of a Cartesian robot is trivially expressed as $P_{ee} = (x, y, z)$ where $x$, $y$, $z$ are the displacements of the three prismatic joints. No trigonometric functions are required in the forward transformation.

#### 2.1.2 Cylindrical Robot (RPP — One Revolute, Two Prismatic)

- **Joint Notation:** **R-P-P** (first joint rotates about a vertical axis, then two prismatic slides)
- **Axis Alignment:** Rotational base + vertical slide + horizontal radial slide
- **Workspace Shape:** A cylindrical volume (annular cylinder)
- **Real-World Examples:** Early Unimate robots, rotation-table assembly stations
- **Advantages:** Good reach for deep insertion tasks (e.g., into a hollow pipe)
- **Disadvantages:** Limited orientation capability, less common in modern industry

#### 2.1.3 Spherical (Polar) Robot (RRP — Two Revolute, One Prismatic)

- **Joint Notation:** **R-R-P** (base rotation, shoulder pitch, radial telescopic extension)
- **Axis Alignment:** Vertical rotation + horizontal shoulder rotation + telescopic reach
- **Workspace Shape:** A spherical sector (portion of a hollow sphere)
- **Real-World Examples:** Unimate 2000 series, foundry and forging robots
- **Advantages:** Large workspace volume relative to footprint
- **Disadvantages:** Complex kinematics, lower accuracy than Cartesian/Cylindrical

#### 2.1.4 Articulated (Anthropomorphic / Revolute) Robot (RRR — Three Revolute Joints)

- **Joint Notation:** **R-R-R** (base rotation, shoulder, elbow — all revolute)
- **Axis Alignment:** Mimics the human shoulder–elbow–wrist anatomy
- **Workspace Shape:** A complex spherical/dumbbell-shaped region with an internal hole (cannot reach behind the base)
- **Real-World Examples:** **ABB IRB, KUKA KR, FANUC R-2000, Yaskawa Motoman** series
- **Advantages:** Maximum flexibility, can reach over and around obstacles, large dexterous workspace
- **Disadvantages:** Most complex kinematics (requires **Denavit–Hartenberg parameters**), lower stiffness

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Board Exam Tip:** Articulated robots are the **most commonly manufactured** robot type in the world (~60% market share in industrial robotics). The famous **PUMA 560** (Programmable Universal Machine for Assembly) is a classic 6-DOF articulated arm.

#### 2.1.5 SCARA Robot (Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arm)

- **Joint Notation:** **R-R-P** with parallel-vertical-axis configuration
- **Compliance Profile:** **Rigid in Z (vertical)**, **Compliant in XY (horizontal)**
- **Workspace Shape:** A flat cylindrical disc
- **Real-World Examples:** **EPSON SCARA, Yamaha YK series, Adept Cobra**
- **Advantages:** Extremely fast (high acceleration, up to **10g**), ideal for vertical insertion tasks (peg-in-hole assembly)
- **Disadvantages:** Cannot reach high above its base plane

#### 2.1.6 Parallel (Delta) Robot

- **Joint Notation:** Multiple parallel kinematic chains (typically 3-RRR + central platform)
- **Workspace Shape:** A dome/hemisphere above the base
- **Real-World Examples:** **ABB FlexPicker, FANUC M-1, M-3** for high-speed packaging
- **Advantages:** Extreme speeds (up to **300 picks/min**), very high stiffness-to-weight ratio
- **Disadvantages:** Limited workspace, complex forward kinematics, many singularities

### 2.2 Classification Based on Degrees of Freedom (DOF)

#### 2.2.1 The Kutzbach–Grübler Mobility Criterion

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The **mobility** (number of degrees of freedom) of a spatial mechanism is computed using the **Kutzbach–Grübler Criterion**:
>
> $$M = 3(N - 1) - 2J_1 - J_2$$
>
> where $M$ is the mobility (DOF), $N$ is the total number of links (including the ground link), $J_1$ is the number of lower-pair joints (1-DOF joints: revolute R or prismatic P), and $J_2$ is the number of higher-pair joints (2-DOF joints: e.g., cam, gear contact).

**Alternative form** (counting only 1-DOF lower pairs):
$$M = 6(N - 1) - 5f_1 - 4f_2 - 3f_3 - 2f_4 - f_5$$
where $f_i$ is the number of joints with $i$ DOF, and the base is counted in $N$.

For a **simple serial chain** with $n$ links and only R or P joints (each with 1 DOF):
$$M = 3(n) - 2(n - 1) - 0 = n + 2 \cdot \text{(redundant)}$$

> **Simplified Rule:** For a serial robotic manipulator composed entirely of single-DOF revolute or prismatic joints, the **DOF equals the number of joints** (since each joint contributes exactly 1 DOF to the chain).

#### 2.2.2 DOF Categories

| DOF Range | Category | Typical Use | Example |
|-----------|----------|-------------|---------|
| **2 DOF** | Planar 2R/2P | Simple pick-and-place | XY plotter |
| **3 DOF** | Planar positioning or 3D translation | PCB loading, light assembly | Cartesian plotter |
| **4 DOF** | 3 translation + 1 rotation | SCARA with single wrist | EPSON LS-series |
| **5 DOF** | 3 translation + 2 rotation | Welding, painting, palletizing | ABB IRB 140 |
| **6 DOF** | Full spatial positioning + orientation | Universal industrial tasks | KUKA KR 16 |
| **7+ DOF** | Redundant manipulators | Humanoid arms, surgery | Da Vinci, FRANKA Panda |
| **15+ DOF** | Humanoid full-body | Bipedal locomotion | ASIMO, Atlas, Optimus |

#### 2.2.3 The 3+3 Rule for Full Spatial Dexterity

> [!NOTE]
> A robot with **3 DOF** can position its end-effector at any point in 3D space (translation along x, y, z). An **additional 3 DOF** is required to orient the end-effector in roll, pitch, and yaw. Therefore, **6 DOF** is the minimum required for **full spatial dexterity** (arbitrary position + arbitrary orientation).

If $N < 6$: the manipulator is **deficient** and cannot achieve arbitrary poses (e.g., SCARA with 4 DOF cannot tilt a screwdriver).
If $N = 6$: the manipulator is **dexterous** and can (in principle) achieve any pose in its workspace.
If $N > 6$: the manipulator is **kinematically redundant**, offering infinite joint solutions for a given end-effector pose — useful for obstacle avoidance.

### 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

The classification of robots is **not merely academic** — it directly drives **system engineering decisions** in modern industry:

- **Automotive welding lines** (e.g., BMW, Tesla body shops) universally deploy **6-DOF articulated robots** because car bodies have complex curved surfaces requiring arbitrary orientation.
- **Semiconductor cleanrooms** use **SCARA and Cartesian robots** for wafer handling because of their **low particulate emission** and **high vertical stiffness**.
- **Food packaging** (e.g., chocolate, biscuit trays) uses **Delta (parallel) robots** because they achieve speeds of **>120 picks per minute** that serial arms cannot match.
- **Surgical theaters** use **7-DOF redundant manipulators** (e.g., Da Vinci) so surgeons can route the tool around anatomical obstacles without colliding with patient tissue.
- **Space-telescope assembly** (James Webb, Hubble servicing) uses **6+ DOF redundant arms** to handle large inertia in zero gravity with smooth trajectory planning.

## SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation 1 — Kutzbach–Grübler Criterion for a Serial Manipulator

> [!IMPORTANT]
> We derive the DOF of a general **spatial serial chain** (open kinematic chain) from first principles.

**Step 1 — Start with the General Spatial Mobility Equation:**

The Kutzbach–Grübler criterion is derived from the constraint counting principle. A rigid body in 3D space has **6 degrees of freedom** (3 translations + 3 rotations). When $N$ links are assembled into a mechanism, the total "free DOF" before constraints is:

$$\text{Total Free DOF} = 6 \cdot N$$

**Step 2 — Subtract the Fixed Ground Constraint:**

The ground link (link 0) is anchored and contributes 6 fewer DOF. Therefore:

$$\text{Total Available DOF} = 6N - 6 = 6(N - 1)$$

**Step 3 — Subtract Constraints Introduced by Joints:**

A 1-DOF lower pair (R or P) introduces **5 constraints** (removes 5 DOF). A 2-DOF lower pair (e.g., universal joint, cylindrical joint C) introduces **4 constraints**. In general, a joint with $i$ DOF introduces $(6 - i)$ constraints.

Let $f_i$ = number of joints with $i$ DOF, where $i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$. Then the total constraints removed are:

$$\text{Constraints} = 5f_1 + 4f_2 + 3f_3 + 2f_4 + 1f_5$$

**Step 4 — Compute the Resulting Mobility (DOF):**

$$\begin{aligned}
M &= 6(N - 1) - (5f_1 + 4f_2 + 3f_3 + 2f_4 + f_5) \\
M &= 6(N - 1) - 5f_1 - 4f_2 - 3f_3 - 2f_4 - f_5
\end{aligned}$$

This is the **generalized Kutzbach–Grübler equation** for spatial mechanisms.

**Step 5 — Specialization for a Pure Revolute-Prismatic Serial Chain:**

If the manipulator has only R and P joints, each contributing 1 DOF, then $f_1 = n$ (total joints), and all other $f_i = 0$. Also, the number of links is $N = n + 1$ (n moving links + 1 ground link).

$$\begin{aligned}
M &= 6((n+1) - 1) - 5n \\
M &= 6n - 5n \\
M &= n
\end{aligned}$$

**Conclusion:** For a simple serial chain composed entirely of single-DOF joints (R or P), **the DOF equals the total number of joints**.

---

### 3.2 Derivation 2 — Workspace Volume of a Cylindrical Robot

**Step 1 — Identify the Workspace Geometry:**

A cylindrical robot (RPP) has three primary joints:
- Revolute base: rotation $\theta \in [0, 2\pi]$ about vertical axis
- Prismatic 1: vertical height $h \in [0, h_{max}]$
- Prismatic 2: radial extension $r \in [r_{min}, r_{max}]$

**Step 2 — Parameterize the Workspace:**

In cylindrical coordinates $(r, \theta, h)$, every point in the workspace is:
$$(r, \theta, h) : r \in [r_{min}, r_{max}], \quad \theta \in [0, 2\pi], \quad h \in [0, h_{max}]$$

**Step 3 — Compute the Volume Element:**

$$dV = r \, dr \, d\theta \, dh$$

**Step 4 — Integrate Over the Workspace:**

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{ws} &= \int_{0}^{h_{max}} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{r_{min}}^{r_{max}} r \, dr \, d\theta \, dh \\
&= \int_{0}^{h_{max}} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \left[ \frac{r^2}{2} \right]_{r_{min}}^{r_{max}} d\theta \, dh \\
&= \int_{0}^{h_{max}} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \frac{r_{max}^2 - r_{min}^2}{2} \, d\theta \, dh \\
&= \int_{0}^{h_{max}} \frac{r_{max}^2 - r_{min}^2}{2} \cdot 2\pi \, dh \\
&= \pi (r_{max}^2 - r_{min}^2) \cdot h_{max}
\end{aligned}$$

**Final Result:**
$$V_{ws,\text{cylindrical}} = \pi \, h_{max} \, (r_{max}^2 - r_{min}^2)$$

---

### 3.3 Derivation 3 — DOF Calculation for a 6-DOF Articulated Robot (RRR + Wrist)

**Step 1 — Identify the Mechanism Components:**

- Number of moving links: $n = 6$ (upper arm, forearm, and three wrist links, plus the base mount)
- Number of joints: 6 (all revolute)
- Ground link: 1

Therefore: $N = 6 + 1 = 7$ (total links including ground), $f_1 = 6$ (six R joints).

**Step 2 — Apply the Kutzbach–Grübler Criterion:**

$$\begin{aligned}
M &= 6(N - 1) - 5f_1 \\
M &= 6(7 - 1) - 5(6) \\
M &= 6 \cdot 6 - 30 \\
M &= 36 - 30 \\
M &= 6
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 3 — Interpretation:**

The result $M = 6$ confirms the articulated arm has **6 DOF**, which equals the number of joints. Each revolute joint contributes 1 rotational DOF about its local axis. These 6 DOF correspond to:
- Joint 1: Base rotation (yaw of base)
- Joint 2: Shoulder pitch
- Joint 3: Elbow pitch
- Joints 4, 5, 6: Wrist roll, wrist pitch, wrist yaw

These 6 axes provide the **3 translations + 3 rotations** required for **full spatial dexterity**.

### 3.5 Worked Numerical Example (KTU Board Pattern)

> **Problem:** A 4-DOF SCARA robot has a base rotation $\theta_1 \in [0, 180°]$, two arm links of length $L_1 = 0.4$ m and $L_2 = 0.3$ m, and a vertical prismatic stroke of $0.2$ m. Calculate (a) the maximum reach, (b) the maximum planar workspace area.

**Solution:**

**(a) Maximum Reach:**

Maximum reach occurs when both links are collinear and extended:
$$R_{max} = L_1 + L_2 = 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7 \text{ m}$$

Minimum reach occurs when the links are folded back:
$$R_{min} = \vert L_1 - L_2 \vert = \vert 0.4 - 0.3 \vert = 0.1 \text{ m}$$

**(b) Maximum Planar Workspace Area (for $\theta_1 = 180°$):**

The reachable annular region has area:
$$\begin{aligned}
A_{ws} &= \frac{\theta_{max}}{2\pi} \cdot \pi (R_{max}^2 - R_{min}^2) \\
A_{ws} &= \frac{180°}{360°} \cdot \pi (0.7^2 - 0.1^2) \\
A_{ws} &= 0.5 \cdot \pi (0.49 - 0.01) \\
A_{ws} &= 0.5 \cdot \pi \cdot 0.48 \\
A_{ws} &= 0.24 \pi \approx 0.754 \text{ m}^2
\end{aligned}$$

**Final Answer:** $R_{max} = 0.7$ m, $A_{ws} \approx 0.754$ m$^2$.

```mermaid
    MED[Medical Field] --> SURG[Da Vinci 7 DOF Surgery]
    MED --> REHAB[Exoskeleton 6 plus DOF Rehab]
    MED --> RAD[CyberKnife Radiotherapy]

    SPACE[Space and Defense] --> ROVER[6 DOF Rover Arm Perseverance]
    SPACE --> ISS[Canadarm2 7 DOF on ISS]
    SPACE --> EOD[TALON EOD Bomb Disposal]
```

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
## SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

> **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**

**Q1.** *Differentiate between a SCARA robot and an Articulated robot. Mention one specific application of each.*

**Model Answer:**

A **SCARA (Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arm)** has a joint configuration of **R-R-P**, with both revolute joints having **vertical parallel axes** and the prismatic joint aligned vertically. Its defining feature is **rigidity in the vertical (Z) direction** and **compliance in the horizontal (X-Y) plane**, which makes it ideal for **vertical insertion tasks (peg-in-hole)** such as **PCB component assembly, screwdriving, and dispensing**.

An **Articulated (Anthropomorphic) Robot** has a joint configuration of **R-R-R** (plus a 3-DOF wrist) with revolute joints arranged in a **shoulder–elbow–wrist** configuration mimicking the human arm. It offers **maximum flexibility and dexterity**, with a 6-DOF version capable of **arbitrary position and orientation** in 3D space. Its primary applications are **arc welding (automotive body shops), spray painting, and complex material handling**.

> **Key Difference:** SCARA excels in **high-speed, vertically-constrained** assembly; Articulated excels in **complex 3D trajectory** tasks requiring orientation control.

---

> **[KTU University Exam – June 2024]**

**Q2.** *Define Degrees of Freedom (DOF) of a robot. State the Kutzbach–Grübler equation for spatial mechanisms and explain each term.*

**Model Answer:**

**Degrees of Freedom (DOF)** of a robot is the **minimum number of independent parameters** (joint variables) required to completely specify the **configuration (position and orientation)** of the end-effector in 3D space.

The **Kutzbach–Grübler mobility equation** for a spatial mechanism is:

$$M = 6(N - 1) - 5f_1 - 4f_2 - 3f_3 - 2f_4 - f_5$$

where:
- $M$ = mobility (DOF) of the mechanism
- $N$ = total number of links (including the fixed ground link)
- $f_i$ = number of joints having $i$ degrees of freedom (e.g., $f_1$ = number of 1-DOF joints such as revolute R or prismatic P)

**Example:** A 6-DOF articulated arm has $N = 7$, $f_1 = 6$ (six revolute joints), giving $M = 6(6) - 5(6) = 36 - 30 = 6$ DOF.

---

### 5.2 Part B — Major Questions (14 Marks Each) — Module Internal Choice Pattern

> **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Model Paper]**

---

#### **Question A (14 Marks) — Geometry-Based Classification**

**(a)** *Classify robots based on geometry. Explain the Cartesian, Cylindrical, Spherical, and Articulated robot configurations with neat sketches, joint notations, and workspace shapes.* **(7 marks)**

**(b)** *A cylindrical robot has a base rotation range of 270°, a vertical stroke of 1.5 m, and a radial extension range of 0.5 m to 1.2 m. Calculate (i) the maximum workspace volume and (ii) the lateral (horizontal) cross-sectional area of the workspace.* **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**(a)** *[Refer to Section 2.1 for the four robot geometry classifications. Tabular summary:]* 

| Robot Type | Joint Notation | Workspace | Joint 1 | Joint 2 | Joint 3 |
|------------|----------------|-----------|---------|---------|---------|
| Cartesian | P-P-P | Rectangular box | Prismatic X | Prismatic Y | Prismatic Z |
| Cylindrical | R-P-P | Cylindrical | Revolute θ | Prismatic Z | Prismatic r |
| Spherical | R-R-P | Spherical sector | Revolute θ | Revolute φ | Prismatic r |
| Articulated | R-R-R | Complex (with hole) | Revolute shoulder | Revolute elbow | Revolute wrist base |

*(Sketches should show a box for Cartesian, a cylinder for Cylindrical, a sphere sector for Spherical, and a multi-link arm for Articulated — 1.5 marks per robot type.)*

**(b)** 

Given:
- Base rotation range: $\theta_{max} = 270° = \frac{3\pi}{2}$ rad
- Vertical stroke: $h_{max} = 1.5$ m
- Radial extension: $r_{min} = 0.5$ m, $r_{max} = 1.2$ m

**(i) Maximum Workspace Volume:**

For a cylindrical robot with limited base rotation $\theta_{max}$ (not full $2\pi$):

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{ws} &= \frac{\theta_{max}}{2\pi} \cdot \pi \, h_{max} \, (r_{max}^2 - r_{min}^2) \\
&= \frac{3\pi/2}{2\pi} \cdot \pi \cdot 1.5 \cdot (1.2^2 - 0.5^2) \\
&= 0.75 \cdot \pi \cdot 1.5 \cdot (1.44 - 0.25) \\
&= 0.75 \cdot \pi \cdot 1.5 \cdot 1.19 \\
&= 0.75 \cdot 1.785 \cdot \pi \\
&\approx 1.339 \cdot \pi \\
&\approx 4.205 \text{ m}^3
\end{aligned}$$

**(ii) Lateral (Horizontal) Cross-Sectional Area:**

$$\begin{aligned}
A_{lateral} &= \frac{\theta_{max}}{2\pi} \cdot \pi (r_{max}^2 - r_{min}^2) \\
&= 0.75 \cdot \pi \cdot (1.44 - 0.25) \\
&= 0.75 \cdot \pi \cdot 1.19 \\
&\approx 2.803 \text{ m}^2
\end{aligned}$$

**Final Answers:** $V_{ws} \approx 4.205$ m³, $A_{lateral} \approx 2.803$ m².

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks) — DOF and Application Classification**

**(a)** *Using the Kutzbach–Grübler equation, determine the degrees of freedom of (i) a 4-DOF SCARA robot and (ii) a 6-DOF articulated robot. Show all steps.* **(7 marks)**

**(b)** *Classify robots based on application areas. Discuss in detail the role of robots in (i) medical surgery and (ii) space exploration, citing at least one real-world example in each domain.* **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**(a)** 

**(i) 4-DOF SCARA Robot:**

Components: 4 moving links (3 arm links + 1 vertical slider), 4 joints (2 R + 1 R + 1 P), all 1-DOF.
- $N = 4 + 1 = 5$ (with ground)
- $f_1 = 4$ (two revolute + one revolute + one prismatic)

$$\begin{aligned}
M &= 6(N - 1) - 5f_1 \\
M &= 6(5 - 1) - 5(4) \\
M &= 6 \cdot 4 - 20 \\
M &= 24 - 20 \\
M &= 4 \text{ DOF}
\end{aligned}$$

**(ii) 6-DOF Articulated Robot:**

- $N = 6 + 1 = 7$
- $f_1 = 6$ (six revolute joints)

$$\begin{aligned}
M &= 6(N - 1) - 5f_1 \\
M &= 6(7 - 1) - 5(6) \\
M &= 36 - 30 \\
M &= 6 \text{ DOF}
\end{aligned}$$

**(b)** *[Refer to Section 2.3 for full application classification.]*

**(i) Medical Surgery — Da Vinci Surgical System:**
The Da Vinci is a **telerobotic surgical system** with **7-DOF redundant manipulator arms** that give surgeons enhanced dexterity, **3D high-definition vision**, and **motion scaling** (tremor elimination). It is used for prostatectomy, cardiac valve repair, and gynecological surgery, with patient benefits including smaller incisions, reduced blood loss, and faster recovery.

**(ii) Space Exploration — Canadarm 2 / Mars Perseverance Rover Arm:**
**Canadarm 2** is a 7-DOF robotic arm on the International Space Station used for berthing visiting spacecraft, moving payloads, and assisting astronauts during spacewalks. The **Perseverance rover** carries a **6-DOF robotic arm** with a coring drill and scientific instruments to collect Martian rock samples — the most complex planetary manipulator ever deployed.

---

### 5.3 Examiner's Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistakes That Cost Marks in KTU Valuation:**
>
> 1. **Wrong joint notation order** — Students often write "PRR" instead of "RRP" for Spherical robots. The convention is **base-to-end-effector order** (joint 1, joint 2, joint 3).
>
> 2. **Forgetting the ground link in Kutzbach calculation** — Always count $N$ as **moving links + 1 (ground)**. A 6-DOF arm has $N = 7$, NOT $N = 6$. This is the **#1 reason students lose 2–3 marks** in DOF problems.
>
> 3. **Confusing "mobility" with "position DOF"** — Mobility is the **total independent parameters**, while a "3-DOF" robot can have 6 mobility if the wrist adds 3 rotations. Read the question carefully.
>
> 4. **Mismatching SCARA and SCARA-like robots** — SCARA's defining feature is **vertical-axis parallelism of the first two R joints**, not just the RRP sequence. The vertical R-R-P configuration is what gives SCARA its selective compliance.
>
> 5. **Application-classification vagueness** — Saying "robots are used in medicine" is worth **0 marks**. Naming the **Da Vinci system** and stating **3 specific benefits** (motion scaling, 3D vision, tremor elimination) earns full credit.
>
> 6. **Workspace formula misuse** — Students often apply the full $2\pi$ cylindrical formula even when the base rotation is limited (e.g., 270°). Always include the **$\frac{\theta_{max}}{2\pi}$ scaling factor** for partial rotation.

---

### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!TIP]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — KTU 2024 Module 2**

- [x] **Six primary geometry classes:** Cartesian (PPP), Cylindrical (RPP), Spherical (RRP), Articulated (RRR), SCARA (RRP-vertical), Delta (parallel).
- [x] **Joint notation convention:** Always written **base → wrist** (joint 1, joint 2, joint 3).
- [x] **Kutzbach–Grübler equation (spatial):** $M = 6(N-1) - 5f_1 - 4f_2 - 3f_3 - 2f_4 - f_5$.
- [x] **Kutzbach–Grübler (simplified, all R/P):** $M = n$ (DOF = number of joints).
- [x] **6 DOF = full spatial dexterity** (3 translations + 3 rotations).
- [x] **>6 DOF = kinematically redundant** (infinite inverse-kinematic solutions).
- [x] **<6 DOF = dexterously deficient** (cannot achieve arbitrary orientation).
- [x] **Cartesian → CNC, 3D printing, pick-place; Cylindrical → die casting, deep insertion; Spherical → forging, spray painting; Articulated → arc welding, automotive; SCARA → PCB assembly; Delta → high-speed packaging.**
- [x] **Workspace formulas:** Cartesian = $2X \cdot 2Y \cdot 2Z$, Cylindrical = $\pi h (R_{out}^2 - R_{in}^2)$, Spherical = $\frac{4}{3}\pi (R_{max}^3 - R_{min}^3)$.
- [x] **Industrial robots dominate 6-DOF articulated architecture** (~60% market share).
- [x] **SCARA is rigid in Z, compliant in XY** — ideal for **vertical insertion** tasks.
- [x] **Delta (parallel) robots achieve >120 picks/min** — fastest pick-and-place class.
- [x] **Da Vinci Surgical System = 7-DOF redundant manipulator** for telesurgery.
- [x] **Canadarm 2 (ISS) and Mars rover arms = 7-DOF and 6-DOF** space-qualified manipulators.
- [x] **Humanoid robots (ASIMO, Atlas) have 15+ DOF** for full-body bipedal locomotion.
- [x] **Cobots (UR5e, Baxter) = force-limited 6/7-DOF arms** for safe human collaboration (ISO 10218).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Final Board Exam Mantra:** "Memorize the **6 joint notations** (PPP, RPP, RRP, RRR, RRP-SCARA, parallel-Delta), the **Kutzbach formula** with the **ground link +1 rule**, and the **5 application domains** (Industrial, Medical, Military, Space, Domestic). These three items alone cover **80% of KTU Module 2 marks**."

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->
